title: Assessing Future Agricultural Flood Risks in China Under Climate Change: Shifting Peaks and Land‐Use Feedback
content:
Abstract

The complex interplay between climate-driven flood hazards and evolving cropland patterns poses a critical threat to food security. Prevailing assessments frequently treat these elements in isolation, overlooking the spatiotemporal feedbacks arising from their dynamic co-evolution. We developed a multi-factor simulation framework integrating various emission scenarios (RCP4.5 and RCP8.5), projected cropland dynamics, and growth-stage-specific flood sensitivity for rice, wheat, and maize. Taking China as a typical case, results reveal a seasonal shift in peak flood losses from July–August to May–June under the adopted modeling framework. This peak shift creates a phenological mismatch that intensifies threats during vulnerable crop growth stages. Compared to RCP4.5, the loss patterns under RCP8.5 exhibit a distinct northward expansion into higher latitudes. Under the RCP4.5 scenario, annual losses are projected to escalate significantly, increasing by approximately 9% by 2050 and over 40% by 2080 relative to the baseline. In contrast, RCP8.5 drives a near-term increase (36% by 2050) followed by a decline to approximately 32% above baseline by 2080, as substantial cropland contraction partially offsets the intensifying climate hazards. The RCP8.5 losses remain approximately 11%–12% below RCP4.5 losses by 2080, reflecting the combined effect of intensified hazard and reduced exposure rather than a convergence to equivalent risk. This study highlights that long-term flood risk emerges from the co-evolution of climate hazards and land use, offering critical scientific support for tailored flood prevention and climate adaptation strategies in China.
